Transcript: On November 18th, 1929, an earthquake of roughly magnitude seven struck under the sea south of Newfoundland, near the edge of the Grand Banks. On land the shaking did little damage, but it set off a tsunami that killed more than two dozen people along the Newfoundland coast. And it did something nobody understood for over twenty years. It broke telegraph cables.

At that time many cables crossed the North Atlantic, and the seafloor south of the Grand Banks was crisscrossed by them. Each telegraph company logged the exact minute a line went dead, so every break was timed. The cables closest to the epicenter failed at once. That was no surprise. But others, farther south and lower down the continental slope, kept working for a while and then failed one after another, the last one roughly thirteen hours after the quake and several hundred kilometers away.

The explanation at the time was that the shaking had made the seafloor slump in many places, or that damaged cables gave way later. Nobody pushed hard on the timing.

Then in 1952, Bruce Heezen and Maurice Ewing, at Columbia University, plotted the break times against distance. The breaks weren't scattered. They marched downslope in order, like something traveling. Their proposal was a turbidity current. Sediment shaken loose on the slope mixes with water, the mixture is heavier than the water around it, and it pours downhill along the bottom, snapping cables as it goes. From the timing, they estimated speeds that may have approached a hundred kilometers an hour on the upper slope, though later estimates are lower.

Geologists had suspected that such currents existed, mostly from experiments in laboratory tanks. What they lacked was one measured in the open ocean. And it turned out they'd had one since 1929, written down minute by minute in the logbooks of telegraph companies.

Transcript: In 1960 the psychologists Jean Berko and Roger Brown described an exchange with a small child who called his inflatable plastic fish his 'fis'. An adult held up the toy and asked, 'Is this your fis?' The child said no. The adult tried, 'Is this your fish?' and the child said yes, his fis. He couldn't say 'sh', but he could plainly hear it, and he objected when an adult said the word his way.

This came to be called the fis phenomenon, and it's taught as a lesson about children's speech. A child's speaking errors don't show what the child knows. Perception tends to run ahead of production. The child has the adult word stored correctly; it's the mouth that hasn't caught up.

That's a real improvement on the older idea that a child who says 'fis' hears 'fis'. But notice it still takes something for granted. It assumes the child's 'fis' and an adult saying 'fis' are the same sound. That's what the adults in the room heard, after all.

Researchers who've recorded children and studied the sound waves, instead of trusting their ears, have found it isn't always so. A child who seems to say 'ring' and 'wing' identically may in fact be making a small, consistent difference between them that adult listeners don't pick up. This is called covert contrast. The child is producing the distinction; it's the adults who are failing to perceive it.

It doesn't happen with every child or every sound. But it matters for speech therapy. If a child is already marking a distinction, the job isn't to teach a new sound from scratch. It's to strengthen one that's already there. So the fis story may have a second layer. The adults were right that the child could hear the difference. They may have been wrong that he couldn't make it.

Transcript: When Leonardo da Vinci painted the Last Supper in a monastery dining hall in Milan in the 1490s, the standard way to paint a wall in Italy was fresco. You spread fresh, wet plaster over a patch of wall and paint into it with pigment mixed in water. As the plaster dries, the color is locked into the surface, and it can last for centuries. But fresco has a strict condition. You can only paint as much as you can finish while that patch is still wet, roughly a day's work, and you can't easily go back and change things.

Leonardo didn't use fresco. He painted on the dry wall, with a binder that seems to have combined egg tempera and oil, over a ground layer he prepared himself. And the painting began to fail almost at once. Paint was already flaking within his lifetime, and by the middle of the sixteenth century visitors described it as badly damaged. It's been restored many times, most recently in a project that ended in 1999.

So, the usual story goes, it was a disastrous experiment, a genius who wouldn't respect the rules of a craft.

But think about how Leonardo actually worked. A writer who knew him described him standing in front of the painting for hours without touching it, then adding a stroke or two and walking away. He revised constantly, building up soft shifts of light and shadow in thin layers. None of that is possible in fresco, where the plaster sets on its own schedule, not yours. A dry wall let him work slowly, go back, and build up the effects he wanted.

In other words, he wasn't ignorant of fresco's rules. He gave up durability to get a way of working that fresco couldn't allow. It cost the painting dearly. But it was a trade, not a blunder.

Transcript: Jethro Tull, the English farmer, not the rock band, is remembered for the seed drill. Around 1700, on his farm in Berkshire, he built a horse-drawn machine that cut channels in the soil, dropped seed into them at a set depth and spacing, and covered it over. Transcript: White-crowned sparrows on the California coast sing regional dialects. A bird near San Francisco sings a recognizably different version of the song from one a few hours' drive away. That alone suggests the song is learned, and in the 1960s Peter Marler, then at Berkeley, set out to find out how.

He raised young males in the laboratory, away from adult birds. Birds kept in complete isolation grew up singing a simplified, abnormal song. So hearing adults matters. Then he played them recordings of adult song through a loudspeaker at different ages. Birds that heard the tapes between roughly ten and fifty days old learned the song well, matching whatever dialect they'd heard. Birds that first heard the tapes later than that learned very little. And birds that were played another species' song, even early, mostly ignored it.

From this came an influential picture: a sensitive period, a window early in life when learning is possible, and an inborn template that steers the bird toward its own species' song. The picture spread widely, including as a model for thinking about human language.

But look at what those birds were given: a loudspeaker. In the wild, a young sparrow hears song from a living bird, one that responds and sings back. In the 1980s, Luis Baptista and Lewis Petrinovich tutored young white-crowns with live adult birds instead of tapes. Under those conditions, birds learned song well after the fifty-day window was supposed to have closed. Some even learned from a live tutor of another species.

That doesn't mean Marler was wrong. Isolated birds really do sing abnormally, and timing really does matter. But some of the limits he measured may have been limits of the tape. A loudspeaker turned out to be a much weaker teacher than a bird, and a window that looked closed may only have been narrowed.

Transcript: Here's a problem every navigator faced before the eighteenth century. To find your latitude at sea, you measure the angle between the horizon and the Sun at noon. With the old cross-staff, you had to sight the horizon and the Sun in different directions from a pitching deck. By the time you'd lined up one, the other had moved. The backstaff, from the 1590s, largely replaced it for sun sights, but you still lined things up by hand while the ship moved, and a small error could put you many kilometers off.

In 1731 John Hadley presented a new instrument to the Royal Society in London. It used two mirrors. You looked straight at the horizon, and by moving an arm you brought a reflected image of the Sun down until it sat right on the horizon line. The key is that both were now in the same view. If the ship rolled, the Sun and the horizon moved together, and the reading held. That's the octant, the ancestor of the sextant.

The story usually stops there, with Hadley. But at about the same time, a glazier in Philadelphia named Thomas Godfrey built a very similar instrument, and his friends pressed his claim. After some argument, the Royal Society seems to have recognized both men as independent inventors.

Then came a surprise. After the astronomer Edmond Halley died in 1742, a description of a double-mirror instrument turned up among his papers. Isaac Newton had written it decades earlier and sent it to Halley, and Halley, as far as we know, never mentioned it.

So who invented the octant? In a sense, all three. But the usual story, with Hadley at the center, holds up. Newton's sat in a drawer. Hadley's was built, tried at sea, and made in quantity by London makers. That is what put it into sailors' hands.

Transcript: In the early nineteen hundreds, Percival Lowell, a wealthy Bostonian who built his own observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, became convinced that there was another planet out beyond Neptune. His reasoning followed a famous precedent. In the 1840s, small irregularities in the orbit of Uranus had led mathematicians to predict where an unseen planet ought to be, and Neptune was found very near that spot. Lowell believed Uranus still wasn't moving quite the way the calculations said, even after Neptune's pull was included. So he worked out a position for what he called Planet X, and his observatory searched for it, without success, until his death in 1916.

Then, in 1930, a young assistant there named Clyde Tombaugh, comparing pairs of photographs of the same patch of sky taken several nights apart, spotted a faint dot that had shifted. It was a new world, not far from where Lowell had said to look. It was named Pluto, and it looked like a triumph of prediction.

Except Pluto was too faint. A body heavy enough to tug on Uranus should have been far brighter. Over the following decades, estimates of its mass kept shrinking, and when its moon Charon was discovered in 1978, astronomers could finally weigh it. Transcript: Here's an experiment from agricultural engineering, of all places. In the late eighteen hundreds, a French engineer named Max Ringelmann had people pull on a rope attached to a gauge that measured force. He tested them alone and in groups of different sizes. You might expect eight people to pull eight times as hard as one. They didn't. As the groups got bigger, the average pull per person went down, and the full group of eight fell well short of what the same eight people produced one at a time.

Ringelmann's own explanation was mostly mechanical. People in a group don't pull at exactly the same instant, or in exactly the same direction, so some of the force is wasted. That's a coordination problem, and it says nothing about anyone's character.

The finding sat largely ignored for decades. Then, in 1974, a team led by Alan Ingham repeated the rope study with a clever change. Participants were blindfolded and told that other people were pulling on the rope behind them. In fact, those others were assistants who only pretended to pull. So each participant was really pulling alone, and there was no timing to get wrong. And yet their pull still dropped when they believed they were part of a group.

That's the turn. Some of Ringelmann's loss was coordination, just as he said. But some of it was people quietly easing off when their own contribution couldn't be picked out. A few years later, Bibb Latané and his colleagues found the same pattern with people clapping and shouting as loudly as possible, and they gave it a name: social loafing.

Later studies found that the effect shrinks when each person's output can be identified, or when people care about the task. So Ringelmann wasn't wrong. He found the half of the explanation that didn't depend on anyone's effort.

Transcript: There's a story historians of cloth like to tell: England tried to shut out Indian cotton, and the ban backfired. It's a neat story, and neat stories deserve suspicion, so let's test it.

In the late sixteen hundreds, England fell in love with a fabric from India. The East India Company was shipping in calicoes, light cotton cloth printed or painted in bright colors that didn't wash out, and nothing woven in Europe could match them. They were cheap and washable, and soon they were everywhere: dresses, curtains, bed covers.

The people losing out were England's wool and silk weavers, the country's oldest protected trades. They petitioned Parliament, and they rioted. In London around 1719 and 1720, weavers attacked women in the street for wearing calico, by some accounts tearing the dresses off them.

Parliament responded twice. A law of 1700 banned printed and painted calicoes from India for use at home. But notice what it left out. Plain white cotton cloth could still come in. So English workshops started buying the plain cloth and printing it themselves. Within a few years, a ban on Indian prints had helped create an English printing trade. So the weavers pushed again, and in 1721 Parliament banned the wearing and use of printed cotton altogether, with exceptions. Even that left room. Cloth woven with linen threads running one way and cotton the other was eventually ruled acceptable, and English producers kept working with cotton.

The bans weren't fully lifted until 1774. Some historians go further and link those decades of trying to match Indian cloth to the spinning machines of the 1760s and 70s. That larger claim is harder to prove.

But the core of the story holds up. The wool weavers won nearly every vote, and the law they fought for planted a cotton printing industry on English soil.

Transcript: If you walk through a salt marsh in New England today, there's a fair chance you'll run into a wall of tall reeds, four meters high in places, so dense you can't see through it. That's Phragmites, the common reed. Over the twentieth century it spread across large stretches of Atlantic coast marsh, crowding out the shorter grasses and rushes, and managers have spent a great deal of money spraying, burning and digging it out.

For a long time, the puzzle was why. Phragmites isn't new to North America. Its remains turn up in marsh peat that's thousands of years old, so it was here long before Europeans arrived. The usual explanation, then, was disturbance: ditching, road building, runoff carrying fertilizer. A modest native plant, the thinking went, had simply been handed conditions in which it could run riot.

Then, in 2002, a researcher named Kristin Saltonstall looked at the plant's DNA, including DNA from herbarium specimens, pressed plants collected over the previous century and a half. She found that the reed taking over the marshes was mostly not the native plant at all. It was a lineage from Europe and Asia that had probably arrived in the nineteenth century, perhaps in ships' ballast, and spread from the coast inland. In many places it had replaced the native reed almost entirely.

So the old view was half right. Phragmites really was ancient here, and disturbance probably did help the newcomer spread. But the plant doing the spreading was an invader.

And that matters on the ground. The native type still survives in scattered patches. It tends to be less aggressive, and often has reddish, glossier stems. A crew that sprays every reed bed it comes across may be wiping out the rarer plant along with the one it means to remove.

Transcript: Most textbooks that cover Roman engineering include the same picture: a cross-section of a Roman road, built up like a layer cake. At the bottom, large flat stones. Above that, rubble bound with lime. Then a layer of finer material, crushed brick or tile mixed with lime. And on top, fitted paving stones, curved so rain runs off. Some versions even give a Latin name for each layer. It looks authoritative, and it's often said to come from the Roman architect Vitruvius.

Here's the problem. Vitruvius does describe those layers, with those names, but he's describing how to make a floor. A paved floor inside a building, not a road. Later writers, especially a French scholar named Nicolas Bergier, who published a long history of Roman roads in 1622, seem to have taken the floor recipe and applied it to highways. And it stuck.

When archaeologists actually dig through Roman roads, they rarely find those four neat layers. What turns up depends on the place. Many roads, especially out in the provinces, were surfaced with gravel, rammed hard over a base of whatever was available locally: sand, chalk, flint, waste from iron working, even timber laid across soft ground. The Romans seem to have drawn this distinction themselves. The historian Livy describes officials in the second century BC hiring contractors to pave the streets of Rome with stone and to surface roads outside the city with gravel.

So the stone-paved highway is real, but it's mostly found near towns and on the busiest routes. The road a traveler walked for most of a journey was probably packed gravel, with a raised, well-drained middle.

The layer cake isn't a fabrication. It's a floor that got promoted. And what made Roman roads last had less to do with a fixed recipe than with using local material well and keeping water out.

Transcript: Starting in the 1930s, the neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield, working in Montreal, operated on people with severe epilepsy. To find which bit of brain tissue to remove, he stimulated the exposed surface of the brain with a weak electric current while the patient was awake. The brain itself feels no pain, so patients could talk to him and describe what they experienced.

Usually what they reported was simple: a tingling in one hand, a flash of light. But occasionally, when he stimulated the temporal lobes, a patient described something far richer. One heard a piece of music, another heard her mother calling, another seemed to be back in a familiar room. Penfield took these as replays of real past experience, and he suggested the brain keeps something like a continuous recording, a strip of film the electrode could play back.

You can see why that idea caught on. It implies nothing is ever truly lost, and that forgetting is just a failure to find the right spot. A survey published around 1980 found that most of the psychologists asked believed something along those lines.
